A bar magnet with its S pole downward falls with initial velocity v0 along the vertical axis passing through the center of the conducting ring. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, a closed conducting ring is fixed horizontally. A bar magnet with its S pole downward, with initial velocity v0, falls along the vertical axis passing through the center of the conducting ring. During the process of passing through the conducting ring, viewed from top to bottom, how does the direction of the induced current in the conducting ring change successively?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a horizontally fixed closed conducting ring, drawn as a horizontal ellipse; a bar magnet moves along the vertical axis passing through the center of the ring, and beside it there is a downward velocity arrow v0. The question stem states that the S pole of the bar magnet is downward, so the lower end of the magnet is the S pole and the upper end is the N pole. Then reason: When the magnet approaches the conducting ring downward from above, the part close to the ring is the lower-end S pole. The magnetic field lines near the S pole point toward the S pole, so the direction of the magnetic field passing through the ring is upward; as the S pole approaches, the upward magnetic flux increases. According to Lenz's law, the magnetic field produced by the induced current must oppose this increase, so the induced magnetic field should be downward. Viewed from top to bottom, the circular current that produces a downward magnetic field is clockwise. After the magnet passes through the conducting ring and continues to leave downward, the part close to the ring is the upper-end N pole side of the magnet; the magnetic flux at the ring can still be regarded as upward, but as the magnet moves away, the upward magnetic flux decreases. According to Lenz's law, the magnetic field produced by the induced current should be upward to oppose the decrease in magnetic flux. Viewed from top to bottom, the circular current that produces an upward magnetic field is counterclockwise. Final answer: first clockwise, then counterclockwise.
